easy.explanation: Ecclesiastes 10:1 compares little foolishness to dead flies that spoil the apothecary’s ointment.
easy.q: What can a little foolishness do to something precious?

easy.explanation: The KJV says, “A wise man’s heart is at his right hand.”
easy.q: Where is the wise man’s heart?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “leave not thy place,” because yielding can pacify great offences.
easy.q: What should a person do when the ruler’s spirit rises against him?

answers: A small fault can ruin something valuable
medium.explanation: The image shows how a small amount of foolishness can damage a good reputation.
medium.q: What does the image of dead flies in ointment teach?

medium.explanation: The fool’s wisdom fails him, and his behavior causes people to say that he is a fool.
medium.q: How is a fool recognized in these verses?

medium.explanation: Yielding means responding gently or giving way, which can calm serious offences.
medium.q: What does “yielding” mean in verse 4?

answers: Both emphasize a calm and sensible response
challenge.explanation: The passage presents wisdom as right direction and self-control, even under pressure from a ruler.
challenge.q: What connection is there between the wise heart and the angry ruler?

answers: The wise man remains steady and prudent
challenge.explanation: The wise person does not act rashly when the ruler is angry, while the fool’s conduct exposes him.
challenge.q: What chiefly distinguishes the wise man from the fool here?

answers: A calm response may prevent the matter from becoming worse
The ruler need not be obeyed
challenge.explanation: The verse teaches that yielding and restraint can pacify great offences.
challenge.q: Why is remaining in one’s place connected with the ruler’s anger passing away?

paragraphs.title: The Danger of a Ruler’s Mistake

easy.explanation: Verse 5 calls it an error “which proceedeth from the ruler.”
easy.q: From whom does the error in these verses proceed?

answers: It is set in great dignity
easy.explanation: Verse 6 says, “Folly is set in great dignity.”
easy.q: What happens to folly under this kind of disorder?

easy.explanation: The KJV says, “I have seen servants upon horses, and princes walking as servants upon the earth.”
easy.q: Who are seen walking upon the earth?

medium.explanation: The passage describes an evil under the sun caused by an error proceeding from the ruler.
medium.q: What can a ruler’s mistake produce?

answers: To occupy a low position or status
medium.explanation: The rich sitting in a low place pictures worthy people being pushed down.
medium.q: What does “sit in low place” mean in this context?

medium.explanation: The verse specifically describes servants on horses and princes walking as servants.
medium.q: What reversal of order appears in verse 7?

answers: It shows a reversal of the proper social order
It explains how horses are trained
challenge.explanation: The unusual positions of servants and princes picture social disorder caused by poor rule.
challenge.q: Why does the picture of servants and princes show the danger of bad government?

answers: It gives a visible example of the disorder described earlier
It changes the subject to money
challenge.explanation: The servants on horses and princes walking illustrate folly being exalted and the worthy being humbled.
challenge.q: How does verse 7 relate to verses 5–6?

answers: Bad leadership can overturn proper ranks
challenge.explanation: The verses show that unjust leadership can raise the unworthy and lower the honorable.
challenge.q: What conclusion about social status is supported by the passage?

paragraphs.title: The Risks of Action and the Advantage of Wisdom

easy.explanation: Verse 8 says, “He that diggeth a pit shall fall into it.”
easy.q: What may happen to one who digs a pit?

easy.explanation: The verse recommends sharpening the edge rather than relying on greater strength.
easy.q: What should a person do when the iron is blunt?

easy.explanation: The KJV says, “Surely the serpent will bite without enchantment.”
easy.q: What may a serpent do without enchantment?

answers: They may bring danger upon the worker
medium.explanation: The digger may fall into the pit, and the person breaking the hedge may be bitten by a serpent.
medium.q: What do digging a pit and breaking a hedge have in common?

medium.explanation: Blunt iron has a dull edge and therefore requires more strength unless it is sharpened.
medium.q: What does “blunt” mean when describing iron?

answers: It saves strength and improves the work
medium.explanation: A sharpened tool is more efficient than using extra force with a dull one.
medium.q: Why is whetting the iron an advantage?

challenge.explanation: Each example shows that an action may turn into danger for the person performing it.
challenge.q: What general idea comes from the examples of the pit, hedge, and wood?

answers: It favors proper preparation over force alone
It forbids the use of tools
challenge.explanation: Sharpening the iron demonstrates that wise preparation makes labor more effective.
challenge.q: How does verse 10 support the value of wisdom?

answers: The harm of speech may be sudden and difficult to stop
challenge.explanation: The verse places the serpent and the babbler together to compare an uncontrolled bite with harmful speech.
challenge.q: What connection is made between a biting serpent and a babbler?

paragraphs.title: The Speech of the Wise and the Fool

easy.explanation: The KJV says, “The words of a wise man’s mouth are gracious.”
easy.q: What characterizes the words of a wise man’s mouth?

easy.explanation: Verse 13 says, “The beginning of the words of his mouth is foolishness.”
easy.q: What is the beginning of the fool’s words?

easy.explanation: The fool’s labor wearies him because he does not know how to go to the city.
easy.q: What does the fool not know how to do?

answers: They begin in foolishness and end in harmful madness
They begin in silence and end in wisdom
They begin in grace and end in peace
medium.explanation: Verse 13 describes a progression from foolishness to mischievous madness.
medium.q: How do the fool’s words develop?

medium.explanation: The phrase describes speech and conduct that are reckless, harmful, and irrational.
medium.q: What does “mischievous madness” describe?

answers: He does not know what will happen or how to reach the city
He speaks only in a whisper
medium.explanation: The fool is full of words but lacks knowledge of the future and practical direction.
medium.q: Why is the fool’s many words unhelpful?

answers: The wise man speaks graciously, while the fool’s speech becomes harmful
The wise man never speaks, while the fool is silent
The wise man is rich, while the fool is poor
challenge.explanation: The passage contrasts the gracious words of the wise with the destructive excess of the fool.
challenge.q: What is the chief contrast between the wise man and the fool?

answers: He speaks much although he lacks true knowledge
He refuses to make any prediction
He knows everything that will happen
challenge.explanation: The fool is full of words even though no one can tell what shall be or what comes afterward.
challenge.q: How is the fool’s uncertainty about the future related to his speech?

answers: The inability to reach a practical goal
A desire to leave the land
challenge.explanation: The expression pictures the fool’s lack of practical direction and inability to reach his destination.
challenge.q: What does “go to the city” represent in the passage?

answers: When its king is a child
When its princes eat at the proper time
easy.explanation: Verse 16 says, “Woe to thee, O land, when thy king is a child.”
easy.q: When is the land described as having woe?

easy.explanation: The blessed land’s princes eat “in due season.”
easy.q: When do the princes of the blessed land eat?

answers: For strength, and not for drunkenness
easy.explanation: Verse 17 says they eat for strength and not for drunkenness.
easy.q: Why do the princes eat in due season?

answers: They pursue pleasure instead of responsibility
They eat at the proper time
medium.explanation: Eating in the morning is presented as a sign of disorder and self-indulgence among the rulers.
medium.q: What is wrong with princes who eat in the morning?

answers: A person of distinguished birth and character
medium.explanation: The phrase describes a ruler of noble standing, in contrast with a childish or immature king.
medium.q: What does “the son of nobles” suggest about the king?

answers: One has immature, self-indulgent rulers; the other has noble and disciplined rulers
One has money and the other has no food
One forbids all work and the other forbids all eating
medium.explanation: The passage contrasts irresponsible rulers with leaders who act with dignity, order, and moderation.
medium.q: What is the difference between the two lands?

answers: It reflects discipline, responsibility, and moderation
challenge.explanation: The timing and purpose of eating reveal whether leaders are disciplined or self-indulgent.
challenge.q: Why does the timing of eating become a measure of leadership?

answers: The importance of proper timing and order
challenge.explanation: The contrast distinguishes careless indulgence from eating at the proper time for strength.
challenge.q: What does the contrast between “in the morning” and “in due season” emphasize?

challenge.explanation: The blessed land is characterized by noble leadership and princes who eat for strength rather than drunkenness.
challenge.q: What quality do the proper king and princes share?

paragraphs.title: Laziness, Enjoyment, and the Power of Money

answers: The house to fill with food
easy.explanation: Verse 18 says, “By much slothfulness the building decayeth.”
easy.q: What does much slothfulness cause?

easy.explanation: The KJV says, “wine maketh merry.”
easy.q: What does wine do according to the verse?

easy.explanation: Verse 19 concludes, “money answereth all things.”
easy.q: What does money answer?

answers: Neglect prevents repairs and causes decay
medium.explanation: A neglected building decays, and through idleness of the hands the house drops through.
medium.q: What is the connection between idleness and a leaking house?

answers: A lack of action or work
medium.explanation: The expression describes inactivity that leaves the house without needed maintenance.
medium.q: What does “idleness of the hands” mean?

medium.explanation: The verse mentions a feast, wine that makes merry, and money that answers all things.
medium.q: What three things are mentioned together in verse 19?

answers: Verse 18 describes neglect, while verse 19 describes provision and enjoyment
Verse 18 praises laziness and verse 19 rejects money
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from the damage caused by idleness to food, gladness, and the usefulness of money.
challenge.q: What contrast appears between verses 18 and 19?

answers: Money can provide for needs, but neglect still causes damage
Money repairs every house without work
Resources have no connection to needs
challenge.explanation: Money can answer needs, but the leaking house shows that diligent action and maintenance are also necessary.
challenge.q: What can be inferred about work and money in this passage?

answers: They illustrate provisions and pleasures money can provide
challenge.explanation: Bread and wine represent food and gladness, while money is presented as a means of meeting many needs.
challenge.q: Why are bread and wine mentioned alongside money?

paragraphs.title: Caution in Speaking Against the Powerful

answers: A worker or a wise man
easy.explanation: Verse 20 warns, “Curse not the king” and “curse not the rich.”
easy.q: Whom should a person not curse?

answers: Even in thought and in the bedchamber
easy.explanation: The warning includes private thought and speech in the bedchamber.
easy.q: Where should one not curse the king or the rich?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “a bird of the air shall carry the voice.”
easy.q: What may carry the voice?

medium.explanation: The verse warns that words spoken privately may be carried to others.
medium.q: Why must a person be careful even with private speech?

medium.explanation: A bedchamber is a private and intimate place, yet even speech there may become known.
medium.q: What does “in thy bedchamber” mean?

answers: They may be revealed and cause trouble
medium.explanation: The voice may be carried and the matter told, bringing consequences to the speaker.
medium.q: What may happen to words spoken secretly?

answers: Even a secret that seems safe may be exposed
challenge.explanation: The image shows how unexpectedly private words may travel and become known.
challenge.q: What does the mention of a bird of the air emphasize?

answers: Cursing the king in thought and cursing the rich privately
Neglecting work and eating too much
Praising the king and obeying the rich
challenge.explanation: The verse warns against cursing the king even in thought and cursing the rich in the bedchamber.
challenge.q: What two kinds of wrongdoing does the warning address?

answers: Speak with caution and restraint about powerful people
challenge.explanation: The verse teaches that even hidden thoughts or words about powerful people may bring trouble.
challenge.q: What practical principle follows from this verse?
